the fifth in the mission: impossible series, starring tom cruise, is entirely action but also highly impersonal.
some have already named this as the best of the series and the one which cements cruise's status as high as james bond or the apex of action stars.

personally, i prefer tom cruise films where he's asked to do more than perform elaborate stunts and where his dramatic chops are tested like in michael mann's collateral (2004) and perhaps his most alarmingly dramatic work in paul thomas anderson's magnolia (1999).

there are also smarter, deeper chase movies than the mission impossible series like minority report (2002).

in rogue nation, cruise resumes his role as ethan hunt, a top secret spy whose group the impossible mission force (imf) is under fire by cia boss alan hunley (baldwin), who wants to dismantle them.
meanwhile, the group is also attacked by a counter organisation called the syndicate, which sends hunt and his team—including benji (pegg)—on the run.
helping hunt escape capture from the opposite team is ilsa (ferguson), who is after a disk with the names of agents on it.
but she remains untrustworthy and elusive for hunt as she keeps switching sides.
hunt's ally agent william brandt (renner) is also on the lookout for him, and trying to escape the increasing pressure from alan, who himself wants to capture hunt.
hunt's mission to find the disk and stop the syndicate organisation takes him global hopping and into scenarios like a night at the opera and also a dangerous infiltration mission under the water.
on top of a female lead, was someone worried renner would further outshine cruise?
for someone of cruise's experience, ethan hunt is not a role which tests him outside of the stunts.

his team regularly mentions their friendship with hunt but there's little downtime to show their bond and any pauses are dedicated towards exposition.

as determined by christopher mcquarrie—who reteams with cruise after directing jack reacher—the content and the shape of the film further dispel hunt's believability.

in one montage or collage of stunts, hunt drowns under water, is revived, speeds off in a car, crashes his vehicle in a series of ridiculous flips, and then he escapes from the wreckage, only to speed off on a motorcycle.
compressing the sequences together makes the film like a cartoon and hard to take seriously, which would be one of the aims of the filmmakers and cruise, who prides himself on the stunts.

one point where the film becomes enjoyable is when it reaches a new height of ridiculousness, as alan gives a speech about hunt being "the living manifestation of destiny." it's an unintentionally hilarious moment, which had a lot of the cinema laughing including myself, but true to form its proceeded by the weight of another chase scene and a knife fight.

tom cruise has already reached his fifties and it'll be interesting to see how the backend of his career treats him and whether he looks for roles that will test his range or at least let him utilise his charisma.

the tom cruise action series rumbles on and does so in a text book tick- the-box fashion - car chases (tick), chases on foot with gun and fights and stuff (tick), chases in the dark (tick), world wide locations (tick), cruise being the only one with the 'vision' (tick), cruise going on the run (tick), subterfuge and deception as standard (tick), the authorities not appreciating cruise and his imf chums (tick), cruise having to do something death defying (tick) several times (tick), cruise on a motorbike (tick), cruise going against the advice of his imf colleagues (tick), guns, lots of guns and gadgets and technology (tick), cruise saving the girl (tick), the day (tick), the world (tick), etc (tick).

the writers appear to have either fallen asleep or just grown lazy when coming up with this one: the cia (boo, hiss) want to close down cruise (hurrah!) and his playmates for not being reliable with saving the world, citing the plots of previous films (breaking into cia headquarters, destruction of the kremlin, the missile that didn't wipe out seattle, etc) to which jeremy renner (as brandt) has to appear before a board of bigwigs and the cia boss (alec baldwin) to argue his case for them not to be closed down (wasn't renner a field agent in the previous movies?
where was their boss anyway?), which the cia want, purely so that they can control an out of control ethan hawk (cruise).

but when the imf (cruise's boys) subsequently gets closed down, and absorbed into the cia, cruise goes underground to carry on his investigation into a group that everyone except cruise (obviously!) believes does not exist.

baldwin decides that cruise has gone renegade and pursues him like there isn't a bigger problem in the world to occupy his time (incidentally, it is unfortunate that the world moves on and baldwin now plays the orange us president on snl, because that was all i could think of in every one of his scenes), even to the point of making it a shoot to kill mission, seemingly because cruise made a fool of him.

there was a beautiful british enemy agent (actually working for the british secret service - or was she?) in a bikini, there was an unemotionally evil criminal boss with a weird voice, there was an evil british government minister with ugly glasses and a dull voice, there were a few evil henchmen who looked as though central casting had been asked to just send some mean-looking east european-looking hombres (own hair not important) along, there was blundering benji and dependable luther to do the technical stuff, warn cruise not to give the secret 'gadget thing' to the opposition and look scared, confused and knowing as required.

like i said earlier, straight out of a text book; sometimes the end result of a scenario was practically telegraphed, it was so predictable.

the mystery came from trying to figure out whether the girl would die before the end of the film, and how the baddie would die (spoiler - he doesn't).

on the dvd there was an additional special feature, a short called cruise control, about (surprise surprise) tom cruise, a little propaganda piece in favour of cruise, with his colleagues (from both in front of and behind the camera) telling us that he was a dream to work with, that he was on the side of the movie goer, that he was dedicated to bringing the best film possible to the viewer, etc.

my eyes glazed over and as a result i missed the end, but it is safe to assume that cruise overcame the baddies, got the girl, and saved the world as usual.

reviewed by filmmining101:

the collaboration between christopher mcquarrie and tom cruise has so far generated three great action films, each one subsequently an improvement in some form over its predecessor.

made by people who love films (and their fans), here we do not have a glorified use of obvious green screens; instead we witness cruise giving it all in fights, car chases, running competitions and stunts reminding the reasons we go to the movies.

offering plenty of cgi free entertainment and bombastic sequences under the complementary grandiose and pulse pounding soundtrack of lorne balfe, this sequel places its bets strictly in the adrenaline department making the most of gorgeous physical locations (e.g., rome, venice) unlike what "fast x" (2023) did.

a two-on-one fight in the narrow streets of venice and a climatic finale involving a luxury train are among the most satisfying action scenes you will see this year echoing the good old days of capturing as many things as possible in film practically and not in a lazy post-production process.

cruise clearly satisfied with mcquarrie's direction, he allows him to tell more engaging storylines for the imf and his likeable but always overwhelmed ethan hunt.

hunt's opponent is not an arms dealer or an agent gone rogue but a faceless antagonist who can do anything at any time highlighting the degree of dependence that the developed world places on algorithms, data and digital technology.

like any of the previous missions, should you choose to accept it, expect a hefty amount of ongoing exposition which in a two and half hour flick can become quickly tiresome.

repeating key moments from the previous installments by putting hunt in situations we have seen him facing before, we are left to wonder where you could possible take this hero after 27 years of cinematic history?

in a sea of mediocrities and uninspired blockbusters filled with digi doubles and sky beams, "dead reckoning part one" wholeheartedly displays its budget at every frame, is gorgeous to look at (especially the night segment in venice lit under a john wickesque cinematography) and cruise carries his charismatic star power throughout a long running time with precision.
you are here to watch cruise delivering a+ blockbuster value and this is exactly what you get.
tom cruise once again delivers what he promised - visually stunning shots combined with amazing stunt work.

ethan hunt is back, defying gravity and expectations in the latest installment of the action-packed mission: impossible franchise.
"dead reckoning part one" delivers heart-pounding set pieces, globetrotting intrigue, and tom cruise's unwavering commitment to physical theatrics.

mcquarrie's direction shines in these moments, balancing elaborate choreography with genuine tension.

at 60, cruise embodies the relentless ethan hunt with unwavering charisma and commitment.

he throws himself into every stunt, making the impossible seem believable (or at least highly entertaining).

rebecca ferguson, hayley atwell, vanessa kirby, and pom klementieff bring depth and intrigue to their roles, forming a formidable team alongside hunt.

the female characters are particularly welcome additions, breaking away from the usual damsel-in-distress tropes.

the central plot, revolving around a deadly weapon and a powerful organization, unfolds methodically, leaving viewers piecing together the puzzle alongside hunt.

with a runtime exceeding two and a half hours, the film occasionally struggles with pacing.

subplots and character development sometimes feel sacrificed for the sake of action set pieces, leading to a slightly bloated feel.

at times, the film relies heavily on dialogue dumps to explain intricate details of the plot, which can feel clunky and interrupt the flow of the action.

while enjoyable, the core structure of the film adheres closely to the established mission: impossible formula, potentially lacking the surprise factor for longtime fans.

fraser taggart's camerawork is dynamic and immersive, capturing the scale and intensity of the action sequences with clarity and flair.

lorne balfe's score keeps the adrenaline pumping, perfectly complementing the on-screen action and suspense.

while mostly seamless, some cgi moments, particularly in the climax, appear slightly less convincing than practical stunts.

tom cruise delivers a typically charismatic and determined performance, showcasing his unwavering dedication to the action sequences.
rebecca ferguson adds vulnerability and complexity to ilsa faust, making her a compelling ally to hunt.

while its overstuffed narrative and exposition dumps might hold it back slightly, the film's stunning stunts, intriguing mystery, and strong performances (particularly from cruise and the supporting cast) make it a worthy addition to the series.

any concerns fans had of the mission: impossible cinematic universe running out of steam 7 films in will be quickly laid to bed when the lights in the cinema dim and the action to this two-part entry takes hold.

ageing like a fine wine and going against the odds stacked against it, the highs of 2018's entry fallout have here been topped with writer/director christopher mcquarrie and his leading man tom cruise combining once more to deliver all you could ever want from an action/thriller of this ilk with covid-19, re-shoot's and gravity unable to hold dead reckoning part one back from becoming one of the must-see blockbusters of the 2023 summer catalogue.

since its humble beginnings in 1996 when brian de palma took a mid-tier tv show to the mainstream, the mission: impossible franchise has continued to up its game and spectacle with each passing instalment and while there's nothing here of great substance or anything that should be taken to heart, there's an undeniable charm, quality and enthusiasm on display here that puts many other counterparts to shame with what this film offers for viewers on an almost non-stop two and half hour plus ride.

featuring the return of everyone's favourite impossible mission completionist ethan hunt and his merry gang of helpers that includes ving rhames luther, simon pegg's benji, rebecca ferguson's ilsa and also new series additions such as shew whigham's always one step behind government agent jasper briggs and pom klementieff's deranged paris, dead reckoning throws a lot of ideas and sequences at us that mostly all land and combine to create a breathtaking thrill ride across the globe.

from an early dalliance in the unforgiving sand swept desert, a thrilling game of cat and mouse in a crowded airport, the years best car chase in the streets of rome right through to a showdown on the famed orient express (featuring the films much hyped bike jump cruise completed for multiple takes), dead reckoning has a large collection of stand out segments that all play out like their own mini-movie with their own narratives taking place and when combined with mcquarrie's pinpoint direction, the films smooth and clean editing and lorne balfe's perfectly bombastic score, this is the very definition of an all-round package that can't be denied.

coming to us at a time and place where many questions are still being asked about the future of cinema and the blockbuster movie making business in general, with a series of 2023 flops tarnishing an industry looking to bounce back from a tough few years, on the back of top gun: maverick and now this film, tom cruise can be seen as a hollywood player that gets what the people want and whether viewers loathe, love or care no way or the other for the seemingly ageless star, there's no denying that if you want spectacle and entertainment that deserves the big screen treatment, cruise has you well and truly covered.

final say -

an endlessly enjoyable and thrilling new entry into a series that is getting better with each passing instalment, mission: impossible - dead reckoning part one is top-shelf hollywood entertainment that leaves most of its peers in the dust as its leading man and director leave us eagerly awaiting next years part two.

imf (impossible missions force) agent ethan hunt (tom cruise, also producing) is assigned to retrieve half of a cruciform key.
ethan travels to saudi arabia where he finds ilsa hiding in the desert, knowing he is the only person she can trust.
ethan believes the entity poses too great a threat to humanity and seeks to destroy it.
agents are searching for ethan, following his actions in washington, and going rogue, but he evades them.
at the airport, ethan sees and recognises terrorist gabriel (esai morales), a figure from his part before he became an imf agent, who is now working alongside the entity.
meanwhile, the half-key is stolen by a professional thief named grace (hayley atwell), who ethan follows on plane to rome, italy.
ethan and grace end up in a chase through the streets, pursued by french assassin paris (pom klementieff), a subordinate for gabriel.
after grace escapes again, ethan reunites with benji, luther, and ilsa.

with support from benji and luther, ethan and ilsa infiltrate a party in venice held by the arms dealer, alanna mitsopolis, aka the white widow (vanessa kirby), daughter of deceased arms dealer max (vanessa redgrave in the original film) who has the other half of the key.
ethan unsuccessfully tries to talk a fearful alanna out of selling it.
gabriel reveals that the entity has infiltrated the party and determined that one of ethan's allies, either ilsa or grace, will die.
ethan tries to find her, but the entity, posing as the voice of benji, sends him the wrong direction.
ethan gets into a fight with paris until he manages to subdue her, but he chooses to spare her life.
gabriel subdues grace and gets into a fight with ilsa, ultimately ending with him fatally stabbing her, and ethan is too late to save her.
grace joins ethan, benji, and luther as she feels remorse for ilsa's death, but luther assures her that she is not to blame.
benji makes a mask for grace to pose as alanna, but when he tries to make a mask for ethan to pose as her brother zola (frederick schmidt), the mask machine malfunctions.
ethan is forced to come up with a new plan to board the train, while luther leaves for an off-grid location to break down traces of the entity in his hard drive.
before leaving, luther warns ethan not to kill gabriel out of vengeance, as only gabriel knows how to use the key.
meanwhile, ethan is on a motorbike having missed the chance to board the train, he is being directed by benji to a way to get onboard.
finally, ethan reaches the edge of a cliff, high above the valley with the train in view, benji says he can parachute onto the train.
ethan backs up and drives the motorbike over the edge, leaping as it descends and deploys his parachute when far enough from the rocks.
he then prepares to kill paris, suspecting she will betray him after ethan spared her in venice, so he stabs her.

ethan goes after gabriel, while community agents jasper briggs (shea whigham) and his partner degas (greg tarzan davis) are also on the train and go after him.
ethan overpowers gabriel atop the train, but jasper and degas corner him before he can kill gabriel, allowing him to jump off the train.
briggs and degas try to get all the passengers to safety, while ethan and grace manage to detach the locomotive from the rest of the train.

mission: impossible - dead reckoning part one is the seventh installment in the long-running spy thriller franchise starring tom cruise as ethan hunt, the leader of the impossible mission force (imf).
hunt and his team, along with some familiar allies and enemies, must race against time to stop the ai from falling into the wrong hands.

along the way, they face deadly traps, double-crosses, and stunning revelations that connect to the very first mission: impossible film from 1996.

rebecca ferguson returns as ilsa faust, hunt's ally and love interest, who has her own agenda and skills.
simon pegg and ving rhames provide comic relief and emotional support as hunt's loyal teammates.
henry czerny reprises his role as eugene kittridge, the former imf director who has a history with hunt.

esai morales plays gabriel, a ruthless mercenary who has a personal connection to hunt's past.

the film also introduces some new characters, such as hayley atwell as kate, a mysterious agent who works with hunt, and pom klementieff as luna, a deadly assassin who works for gabriel.

fresh off his cinema-saving success with top gun: maverick, cruise (and director christopher mcquarrie) comes back with another giant summer tentpole film - mission impossible: dead reckoning, part one - and they hit it out of the park again.

the 7th film in the mission impossible franchise (which debuted, incredibly, 27 years ago), dead reckoning, part one reunites ethan hunt (tom cruise) with his band of hero/outlaws to stop yet another world-wide crisis.

it's familiar ground but it is the journey not the destination that makes these types of films work and the journey (which, to be honest, is just an excuse to jump from action set piece to action set piece) is a fun one filled with comfortable characters/actors both old and new.

besides cruise (who's got the ethan hunt character down), dr1 is filled with hunt's "regular" crew, luther (vingh rhames - the only other actor besides cruise to be in every mi film), benji (simon pegg - around since mi 3) and ilsa faust (rebecca ferguson - on board since film 5).

all bring their "a" game to the adventure and all of them acquit themselves just fine.

oh...and henry czerny reprises his role as kittridge from the first mission impossible film - and it was good to see him, too as was vanessa kirby's re-appearance as hunt's "frenemie", the white widow (in a role that is a bit more expanded).

but, of course, all of these actors/performances takes a back seat to the action sequences and mcquarrie and cruise are at the top of their game here.

unlike another big action flick (that leaned more towards the over-the-top comic-book type action), this mission impossible film relies on tension to make these action scenes pop off the screen - and mcquarrie succeeds.

since this film is labeled as "part one" you would expect to this film to end on a cliff-hanger and mcquarrie/cruise were smart about that, too.

mission impossible's dead reckoning part one brings back the iconic tom cruise as the fearless ethan hunt, joined by an exceptional ensemble cast including hayley atwell, rebecca ferguson, vanessa kirby, and a host of other talented actors.
while tom cruise's performance continues to be exemplary, the film's story falls short of its potential.

nevertheless, the film manages to retain its allure, thanks to the unwavering charisma of tom cruise as ethan hunt.

one of the film's most significant drawbacks is its excessive length, as it could have benefitted from tighter editing to maintain a more captivating pace and keep the audience fully invested in the unfolding events.

in conclusion, mission impossible's dead reckoning part one offers a mix of highs and lows.
tom cruise's stellar performance and some standout action scenes add excitement and spectacle to the film, but the repetitive storyline and lack of fresh ideas dampen its overall impact.

also, the close ups of tom cruise were a bit painful with his hair not appearing properly made for the close shots like dry and poorly trimmed and styled.

it had the parodish feeling of terminator: dark fate and the length that felt like an extended lord of the rings film dvd/bluray release.

but tom and co seemed to get around it ok.

unless you have been living under a rock, you know what this franchise is about, and thus you know pretty well what you are going to get.

gabriel was good, but thus idea that he is somehow working for the entity, almost in sync with its "thought process" really didn't land for me, i think the idea was that we viewed them as counterparts to one overall enemy force but instead it felt like both were actually rather hindered by each other instead of complimentary which really took the edge off any real feeling of threat.

the two american cia guys (at least i think they were cia) were very jarring and didn't need to exist at all outside of the airport scene, i enjoyed greg davis despite his small part, but shea wighams character was terrible and totally miscast (was he supposed to be taken seriously?)

talking of not making much sense, there was an over abundance of exposition where it wasn't required, one of the greatest things about the mission impossible franchise is that it doesnt spell it out for you, and this makes figuring it out for yourself far more rewarding, and queues up great twists, there is none of that in this, intact i dont think there was a single plot twist whatsoever, or at least nothing that wasn't instantly obvious a mile off.

the car chase sequence was cool for stunts, but didn't actually need to be in the film whatsoever, it just served as a platform to setup gabriel's henchwoman paris and to get away with some stunts, also if they really did drive that armoured truck off the balcony why the hell didn't they show it?

circling back round to stunts, the main stunt of the movie (which is great) you have already seen in its entirety in the trailer, which jarred me quite a lot, i think one of the best things about the stunts in the previous outings was that you follow them from beginning to end, in this one it's 10 minutes of occasionally cutting to tom riding up a mountain on a bike, to the stunt you have already seen, to him (completely out of the blue) being on the train at exactly the right place and time, i know this is mission impossible but that jumped the shark.

the train sequence is good, particularly the last bit, but it's too long, also if they really did crash that train the choices of how that were shot were terrible, sure a single snap cut to an on-board of it heading down mid-drop would make sense, but not having a wide shot was a really bad decision.

the alleyway fight that seems to be getting a lot of praise failed to capture me to be honest, you couldn't see what the hell was going on and tom could of very easily got out of their almost instantly, also there is no reason why he didn't kill paris, its purely because its required that she be alive at the end.

maybe i'm being overcritical, but i'm being honest, this is a good fun action film, it isn't a mission impossible film though and unless there are elements in part 2 that relate to unforseen elements of this one its essentially filler, while we wait for the grand finale, this entire film could of been condensed into 30 minutes pretty much and stuck on the front of part 2 and it wouldn't of made any difference.

where john wick 4 was two films cut down and condensed into one, this is what should of been one film strung out into two, and it shows.

i think simon pegg's character, "benji dunn" summed up the 7th instalment in the mission impossible franchise best when he uttered these words, "details get in the way".

and it's true with "mission impossible: dead reckoning part one" details do get in the way of this almost non-stop action, adventure, thriller under christopher mcquarries' direction.

the mcguffin in this movie is a key made of two parts that unlocks a sentient computer called "the entity" which is nefariously destroying the digital age.

problem is your mcguffin is usually an object, event, or character in a story that lacks intrinsic importance, but serves to set and keep the plot in motion.

meaning it can't also be your stories antagonist.

all i can say is i'm glad i wasn't playing a drinking game with the words "key" or "entity" in it or i would have died from alcohol poisoning.

talking trains even agatha christies stylings are up for grabs on this orient express train ride to hell.

by the way, train spotters don't cry for what happens to the train that appears to be a preserved britannia class steam locomotive (curiously disguised as a french engine) in fact, it's actually a specially commissioned non-functioning stunt replica.

and if you get confused on how rome suddenly becomes venice with boats etc, it's because filming started in venice on the same day northern italy locked down for covid-19.

production was hastily moved to rome, only to be shut down again.

gotta love a pandemic for messing up a movie shooting schedule.

the frequent delays caused by covid-19 ballooned the budget to $290 million, making it the most expensive mission: impossible film, and the most expensive film of tom cruise's career.

mission: impossible: dead reckoning part one (2023) : movie review -

tom cruise and christopher mcquarrie's pair bring another thrilling adventure in the mi series with mission: impossible - dead reckoning part one.
if i am not wrong, then cruise and mcquarrie's collaboration (in any way) hasn't gone wrong except for "the mummy" (2017).
rather, christopher mcquarrie is responsible for writing and directing one of the best films in tom's filmography.
ethan hunt is given a task to find a key from his friend, ilsa faust (rebecca ferguson).
in the next scene, we travel from the ocean to an arabian desert, where ethan confronts ilsa and eventually gets the key.
the key has to be traded, so ethan shakes hands with a pickpocket, grace (hayley atwell), who is actually working for the opposite party.
after quite a thrilling smackdown session at the airport, grace takes the key to venice, and as expected, ethan, luther (ving rhames), and benji (simon pegg) follow her there to get it.
gabriel has some plans written that ethan has to deal with, but it's pretty difficult this time since the ai thing, the entity, knows it all.
will ethan and his team get what they want?
so it's impossible to imagine that hunt might not get out of that situation.
grace's character is annoying at times, but it's more frustrating to see even a smart character like hunt not knowing it.

mi 7 goes through all those mainstream elements you have been seeing for years or may be anticipating from a regular spy thriller.

tom cruise is ethan hunt, and he still believes it in 2023, just like he did in 1996.
ethan definitely needs some updated theories to deal with his opponents instead of going back to the old house and going back in time.
cruise and his action team deliver enough entertainment despite repetitive flaws.
i'd like to believe that ethan hunt still has enough fuel left.
this is the first movie where tom cruise seems less confident, unsure and slower.

granted he is 60, however after all ethan hunt has been through, you'd think he'd be more revered and knows what to do.

i felt like half of the movie was him chasing after haley atwell who played the pick pocket.

they spent several movies building up her character, only for her to die so simply while tom was doing his long sprint scene, which there isn't a shortage of in this movie.

the main villain is ai.
no real life foe we are accustomed to that tom can have an epic battle with at the end.
the beginning was awkward, starting with ethan hunt's first appearance, but especially with the scene where the ai threat-or rather, the premise of this movie-is explained in a theatrical style.

thankfully, at that moment, tom cruise delivered a significant shift in the movie's pace and, above all, in its narrative, bringing us back to what defines this franchise the most.

however, the plot crossed the line into absurdity, which, combined with gabriel's lackluster character, made the story not only clichéd and forced but also devoid of charm.

essentially, they follow the same formula every time: they discard one love interest, introduce another, bring in a new boss hunting ethan, and a talented villain who appears out of nowhere.

in this specific case, gabriel appears out of nowhere as if he were an old acquaintance of ethan, which is frustrating because they created something from nothing instead of weaving it into the narrative of the previous six films.

the mi enthusiasts rush to give it 10 stars and get all defensive with people who try and rate it critically.

i really like tom cruise other than maybe his religious tendencies, but he really isn't a very good actor and he pales compared with the likes of daniel craig and matt damon.

but, he can carry a film on his charisma, likability and his incredible guts in delivering his own stunts.

make no mistake, this movie is state of the art when it comes to stunts and special effects.

but in their haste to make jaw-dropping effects the makers completely forget to write a coherent script.

there were some amusing one-liners, but by and large it felt like it was a race to get to the next action sequence so the scriptwriters could go back to drinking coffee and staring into space.

as such the character development was negligible and the film felt super shallow (which of course, it is).

and the insistence in every scene where these was dialogue with more than two people to rotate the lines equally felt like an in-joke.
its been a long time coming this film and as i said the stings are very good and no doubt cruise done them all himself or most of them but just lacking for me.
they've spent two films building up ilsa as being ethan's equal, and hinted at an eventual romance.

with the seventh film in the series, and the third straight he has directed, writer-director christopher mcquarrie and superstar actor and daredevil tom cruise have managed to accomplish what seemed unlikely ...
they have delivered ethan hunt's biggest and grandest mission yet.
of course, we are only one year removed from tom cruise's top gun: maverick being credited with 'saving cinema', so stay on alert for a 'sky is falling' panic.

mcquarrie co-wrote the script with erik jendresen ("band of brothers"), and they remain faithful to the characters and storylines established by the tv series creator, bruce geller.

there may never have been an actor more suited to a recurring role than tom cruise as ethan hunt (harrison ford as indiana jones might be the closest).

your questioning of how a 'simple' spy-thriller can be effective is understandable, yet it's fascinating to watch as ethan hunt's mission in life as an agent is evaluated, as is the cost he's paid as a man.

and lest you be worried, there are enough cruise sprint scenes here to put chariots of fire to shame.

familiar faces include ethan hunt's team of luther (ving rhames, who along with cruise, has appeared in all 7 mi films), benji (simon pegg), and ilsa faust (rebecca ferguson).

new faces include haylee atwell as master pickpocket grace, whose soul may or may not be beyond salvation; cary elwes as agency director denlinger; shea whigham and greg tarzan davis as officers after rogue hunt; and pom klementieff as a hired assassin.

the stunt work here is outstanding, and of course, tom cruise is renowned for personally handling many of the most breathtaking acts - the most memorable one here being his riding of a motorcycle off a cliff.
cruise was 34 in that one.

it's a mission that will be closed out in part two, and simultaneously bring an end to cruise's remarkable run as ethan hunt.

opening july 12, 2023.

i am a fan of tom cruise and especially his mission impossible series, i have personally enjoyed and watched this series over and over again.

tom cruise, who has been elevating the quality of action films he stars in during recent years, manages to push the genre to the top from a technical perspective in his latest action flick, mi7, despite some script shortcomings.

regarding camera work, it is the best i have seen since john wick 4.

simultaneously, ethan fighting two people in a tight spot exemplifies how well fight choreography can be executed when needed.

in terms of acting, i didn't witness extraordinary performances, but tom cruise continues to improve.

we can't thank him enough; he is tirelessly keeping this genre and the industry alive.

as for the script, i believe there are occasional clichéd and simplistic solutions when ethan finds himself cornered and desperate.

the film's production coincided with the pandemic, making it a real challenge, but the director and the entire team managed to put in a lot of effort and deliver a distinctive film despite some script deficiencies and shortcuts (for example, that famous scene where ethan jumps from the mountain and finds grace's troubled wagon in the 10-carriage train and enters through the window).

you'll find chases, crashes, races around rome, as baddies start to hunt and seek and comb, at an airport crafts reveal, a game that's all about the steal, now you see it, now you don't, you're not alone.

while the movie delivers a solid dose of adrenaline-fueled excitement, it falls short in capturing the essence of what makes mission: impossible so beloved.

let me clarify, the jaw-dropping stunts and action sequences are some of the best we've seen in the entire series, showcasing the incredible skills of ethan hunt and his team.

"fallout" had set the bar high, offering not only exhilarating action but also meaningful character arcs, especially in ethan's relationships with ilsa and julia, which provided a satisfying sense of closure.

in dead reckoning: part one, the movie stretches itself across two films, but it feels like an overdose of relentless action spectacles at the expense of character growth.

there is a scene towards the end where a certain train is falling, and that was easily one of the most creative and intense action set pieces in recent times.

haley atwell's performance (other than tom cruise, of course) stood out in this movie and her character was a great addition to this franchise.

there are still things i didn't like though.

except for tom cruise?

mission: impossible - dead reckoning part one is a rollercoaster of espionage and adrenaline, and as a die-hard fan, i was ecstatic to join ethan hunt on his seventh mission.

dead reckoning part one introduces a more well-rounded approach, infusing humor into the high-stakes proceedings.

whether it was tom cruise's iconic running sequences or the elaborate stunt that finds ethan launched several thousand feet off the ground to land on a moving train.

for a rating, i would give this movie a 8 out of 10.

my rating falls just under a ten because i felt that the plot of the movie was very much driven by the same event in the other movies, which was the death of a female character that happened to be the l,ove interest of ethan hunt.
although killing his love interest adds more to the plot and gives ethan another layer of passion for meeting his objective, the death only seems to propel the male lead.

a classic example of the fridging trope, the female characters who meet a tragic ending in this movie are barely developed outside of their interactions with ethan hunt, which was disappointing for me.

the film started off great with a polished submarine opening and ethan finding his way back to imf, but apart from a few other standout scenes this one feels emptier than the great films that came before it.

one of the biggest issues is that the latest mi felt like it was working to check off all the boxes on a running list of espionage/thriller tropes while also intentionally or unintentionally borrowing many iconic things from the james bond films.

the story is also messy and adds some new points that feel like last minute additions to a two part ending for tom cruise's ethan hunt.

looking past those issues, it really is a fun movie with some incredible moments.

hayley atwell as grace i found a little nauseating in the early scenes constantly giving ethan the slip, but i acknowledge that's just me and my personal preference!

it's got the glamour and opulence from the global destinations on show, pulsating action scenes and the comic touches at inappropriate moments that we've come to expect from mission impossible, and i'll certainly be anticipating the second part hitting the big screen.

the work done in the last years with "ghost protocol", "rogue nation" and "fallout" is remarkable, and "dead reckoning" fits perfectly in this virtuous path, giving the fans a spectacular and very entertaining movie.

the prologue sets up the story very well and presents ethan hunt's mission to recover two halves of a key capable, when together, to unlock unknown and world-changing powers for their owners.

dead reckoning does not do that mistake at all.

for the first time in the franchise, ethan and his team are confronted not only with a human villain (gabriel), but also with fully digital one.
these are very exciting and brilliantly made, and tom cruise does exceptionally in these.
one of the themes of the movie, even if not really new in the mi legacy, is that this mission is going to involve and put in danger the people ethan cares the most about.
"ethan, this mission is gonna cost you...dearly" (kettridge).

spending a bit more time on the characters and on ethan's relationship with them would have made this theme more original and real: we could have seen how much ethan cares about his friends, instead of just knowing it, we could have connected a bit more on an emotional level with the things at stake.

tom cruise reprises his iconic role as the relentless spy, ethan hunt, in the latest instalment of the mission: impossible series.

in this adrenaline-fueled adventure, hunt embarks on a high-stakes mission to retrieve the cruciform key.

this key is the only way of unlocking the source code of the rogue ai.

from the beginning, the film grabs viewers' attention and catapults them into a whirlwind of action and thrilling moments.

it is like a screenwriter trying to make its way to the final chapter.

the entity uses one and then the other, but of course, it fears a character: ethan hunt (obviously).

therefore, there is concern from the ai that it must get rid of him.

there is a scene where the imf heroes try to predict the ai's calculations and make ethan hunt promise not to kill the villain because it is an acceptable scenario for the ai.

ethan hunt understands and swears not to kill him, he says it through dialogue - as for the audience but also because the ai obviously listens to conversations, perhaps through phones.

then comes the final duel, and what happens?
ethan hunt decides at the last second that he will still kill the villain, even though it makes no sense from a narrative standpoint and everything will be lost, it blows up the plot.
but ethan hunt is exactly what the ai cannot tolerate: unpredictability.

the ai realizes this although only the audience has seen her reaction in venice after the fight with ethan hunt, the ai calculates the probability and finds this: pom will betray the group, so it orders the villain to preemptively kill her, even though she herself didn't know she would go that far (she explicitly states after receiving the almost fatal blow that she is surprised that the villain's reason to kill her was because she would betray him, and that he was right - no one would have expected a furious character like paris to betray the bad guys as she seemed the most evil and crazy from the start, it was a complete shock but that is the point).

in fact, within the screenplay or the filmmaking itself, the ai acts as a screenwriter of a mission impossible film, calculating plot points.

ethan hunt is the hero, he is the one who makes decisions that disrupt the causes and consequences until he breaks free from the plot and saves people.

furthermore, the opening credits consist of a trailer showcasing all the scenes we are about to see (as was done in a certain serial era).

and also the trailer as a device.

it may not reach the level of a kubrick film where everything aligns perfectly, but it's present, it is explicit, and it's amusing to see further with this film, whether the movie can claim a potentially underestimated depth.

the ai is the script of the mission impossible charade, and ethan hunt is the one who must break free from the walls.

well the summer finally hits the cinema after a string of bombs, and tom cruise saves the day once more, just like he did with tg: m last year.

and what a hoot the film is, from beginning to end.

it's very silly, and there are a few times when you really have to suspend disbelief, but it works, just about.

cruise as always is excellent as hunt, and he knows the character inside out, and this film shows his foibles, his weaknesses, and the rest of the team are as essential as always.

the imf team is essential to the films foundation, and they seamlessly bounce off each other, just like previous instalments.

action, there is plenty of it, and there are a few standout set pieces, such as the prolonged care chase with the 'hilarious' fiat 500, and of course, what the trailer has partially spoiled, that stunt, and a wonderful final set piece , which reminded me of the first mi film, the lost world: jurassic park, and even dial of destiny to some extent.

balfe returns with an exceptional score, and the film as a whole, really doesn't give you much chance to catch your breath, as every minute is essential to the plot and the narrative.

say what you like about cruise, he has been the most consistent big name in the last 35 years, and his films are always an event.

mission: impossible - dead reckoning part one (2023) review

tom cruise returns as ethan hunt in mission: impossible - dead reckoning part one, delivering another high-octane thrill ride that solidifies the franchise's reputation for breathtaking action and jaw-dropping stunts.

directed by christopher mcquarrie, this installment raises the stakes with a gripping story, a formidable new villain, and some of the most spectacular set pieces in the series' history.

plot & execution the film follows ethan hunt and his imf team as they race against time to track down a powerful ai weapon known as "the entity" before it falls into the wrong hands.
with global security at risk, hunt faces off against shadowy forces, including the enigmatic gabriel (esai morales), an adversary with ties to his past.

the screenplay balances high-stakes drama with well-placed humor, never losing sight of its core emotional themes-loyalty, sacrifice, and the weight of ethan's choices.

action & stunts the mission: impossible franchise is known for its practical stunts, and this film does not disappoint.
from a white-knuckle train sequence to a mind-blowing motorcycle jump off a cliff (performed by cruise himself), the action sequences are nothing short of breathtaking.

mcquarrie's direction ensures that every moment feels immersive, with crisp cinematography capturing the tension and spectacle.

performances & characters tom cruise once again proves why he is one of hollywood's last true action stars, bringing unwavering intensity and charisma to ethan hunt.

and then there's a set of unknown aspects, that with brilliance and creativity, they fill with light-hearted comedy, drama, captivating action and thriller.

the new characters are refreshing, the dynamics between ilsa and ethan had long become exhausting.
typing this at the end of the movie in the theater: ethan hunt and his team continues an ever exciting and nerve wracking journey to do the work that no one else dares to do.

a cruise-ing triumph with wheels

tom cruise returns as the ever-defiant ethan hunt in the seventh installment of the mission: impossible franchise, dead reckoning part one.

cruise, as always, commits fully to every death-defying feat, and the film's stunt team deserves a standing ovation for crafting some of the most pulse-pounding sequences in recent memory.

the grand prix of car chases

but the crown jewel of the action is undoubtedly the car chase sequence that takes place through the winding streets of rome.

the themes of global threats, technological warfare, and the price of loyalty resonate in our current climate, adding a layer of depth to the adrenaline-fueled action.

cruise controls the show

tom cruise is, as always, the anchor of the film.
his ethan hunt is a charismatic blend of action hero and vulnerable soul, and cruise delivers a performance that's both thrilling and emotionally resonant.

the supporting cast, including the always-excellent rebecca ferguson and the delightful newcomer hayley atwell, provide able backup, but it's cruise who truly owns the screen.

verdict: a must-see for action fans

in "m:i - dead reckoning: part 1", ethan hunt (tom cruise) faces an artificial intelligence that started as an assistant to the american government, but ended up learning on its own as it worked and transformed into a deadly sentient creature, willing to predict future panoramas and find ways to eliminate them, guaranteeing their existence.

hunt needs to gather his usual collaborators, as well as a talented thief (hayley atwell) to reach his opponent gabriel (esai morales), who may hold the two halves of a key capable of opening the new global weapon.

a good example of this is the escape scene between improvisations and changing vehicles that ends with a comical number between grace (hayley atwell) and ethan driving in circles in a beetle through the streets of rome and venice.
ethan brings together the usual team, is faced with puzzles that are practically impossible to put together and once again becomes the key to saving the world.
mcquarrie decides to elect gabriel (esai morales), someone who hurt ethan in the past, as a bodily extension of the entity.

the result is that neither artificial intelligence is elaborated as a global threat nor the rivalry with the flesh-and-blood nemesis is convincing on a dramatic level.

that said, the film is built around this epic clash between man and machine, showing that tom cruise is willing to face computers on and off the screen.
previously considered just a hollywood heartthrob, cruise has established himself as the main name in current action and makes every second on screen count.
his ethan hunt comes naturally and continues to impress with his sense of escapism.
grace, played by hayley atwell, is an international thief who crosses ethan's path for the object needed to intercept the machine.
now, together with hunt, she needs to escape henchmen who are really looking for the a.

obviously, there are digital touches in some moments, but nothing that takes the focus away from seeing stuntmen or tom cruise himself actually throwing himself off a cliff, as this man increasingly makes me believe that he wants to die in front of a team of filming, but just don't know how.

at one point, for example, hunt and his allies need to intercept a suspicious sale at an airport, and the mission is to find the target, recover the item (a piece of a key, related to the entity) and escape without being noticed.

for almost three hours, "settlement" offers constant tension, and it is even necessary to take a breather when leaving the theater, especially due to the megalomaniacal scope of the sequences.

since the third chapter, the franchise has become defined by tom cruise's insanities.

seeing him run, jump his motorbike off a mountain peak, escape in a compact cinquecento through italian streets, or even climb onto the top of a moving train, are great reminders that cruise is willing to do anything in the name of the crazy grandeur that only cinema can deliver.

tom is acting and supervising everything in the action sets to perfection with an expenditure of $280 million for stunts alone!

when you settled that this action scene must be the peak moment of the movie then there comes another one!

this time, cruise's ethan hunt isn't fighting nihilistic terrorists or vaporous international-espionage networks but an all-powerful artificial intelligence known as "the entity" that has instant access to any and all online networks and can effectively dupe the world's tech-reliant militaries into fighting one another.

it's a variation on the man-versus-machine theme that cruise and mcquarrie pursued in last year's top gun: maverick and a rather compelling metaphor for their well-publicized dedication to old-school action film-making and real-life stunt work.

alec baldwin's alan hunley once memorably called ethan hunt "the living manifestation of destiny"; this time, shea whigham's jasper briggs, (yet) an(other) intelligence agent tasked with bringing hunt in, describes him as "a mind-reading, shape-shifting incarnation of chaos." everybody is set in their usual roles.
rebecca ferguson's ilsa faust is once again a cross between love interest and mysterious outsider, a rogue spy who has to save ethan and be saved by him at key moments.

hayley atwell's grace, a professional thief who winds up entangled in the attempt to retrieve two halves of a mysterious key that everybody's after, makes for an energetic audience surrogate, and she and cruise have excellent chemistry.
whenever it gets down to the business of making tom cruise run and jump and drive and fly in and out of things, dead reckoning manages to astonish.
tom cruise were able to successfully finish another good movie in a short period of time, after top gun.

mission: impossible - dead reckoning part one picks off nearly five years from the masterpiece of fallout to bring us the penultimate movie of a grand two-part farewell for ethan hunt and his team.

we are lucky to have the likes of cruise and his longtime collaborator, director christopher mcquarrie.

cruise and mcq produce this highly intense spy thriller to another level, by choreographing a perfect blend of excellent directing, cunning writing, huge stunts, clever production design, and superb acting.

with the mission: impossible series turning 23, it has come a very long way from the campy action flick mission: impossible, to the dark, perfectly narrated mission: impossible - dead reckoning, the seventh film in the series.

m:i 7 has all the trademarks of a mission: impossible film - dangerous missions, intrepid characters, groundbreaking daredevil stunts (most of which are performed by tom cruise himself), and some humor sprinkled in the mix.

the characters go through excellent development - the brother-sister relationship of ilsa and ethan, to the friendship between luther and benji, to the smooth arc of the franchise's newest female lead - hayley atwell's grace.

it is fascinating, even magical, how tom cruise's films keeps bringing us back to the theatres.

so, i tip my hat to you, mr cruise, for your exceptional work in almost every genre, and the magnetic power you wield over every film freak on planet earth.

in turns nail-biting, introspective, heartwarming, heartbreaking, comic and diabolical, m:i 7 has everything you'd ask for in an action film, and so much more, but even then one feels disappointed that it has to end.

mission: impossible dead reckoning begins with a submarine believed to be targeted by an invisible enemy setting in motion the events which reveal the macguffin, a halesque sinister force and a world facing not only the external threat of its own data-collecting systems but an internal one spurred by the temptation of man in his desire for power and control.

what follows is a mission: impossible film in every sense which is replete with high stakes, car chases, beautifully choreographed fight scenes and locations that take on a life of their own reflecting the imf team's emotional journey and the pacing of the film at every corner.

the deserted runes of rub al khali in abu dhabi are perfect for two isolated agents, ilsa (rebecca ferguson) and ethan to find one another, just as the densely-populated abu dhabi airport offers an espionage meet-cute in a crowd of strangers amid a crisis of bogdanovich proportions as benji (simon pegg) faces his fears while trying to track a suspicious package that reveals more about himself than he bargained for.

in a nod to "what's up doc?" with undertones of "the thomas crown affair", tom cruise's ethan meets his match in grace, played to perfection by hayley atwell as the apparent petty thief who has more identities than an imf agent and even more sass to spare.

the streets of rome provide a picturesque backdrop to pick up the pace as grace and ethan find themselves struggling in a hilarious and nail-biting chase scene involving a small yellow fiat providing the perfect set-up for close encounters of the screwball situational kind in one of the film's many humorous highlights.

venice is the heart and core of the movie, providing a tapestry of haunting emotional scenes that push ethan to the point of no return as he faces his greatest fears and the loss of those he considers kindred ghosts, floating in and out of the world around them ensuring order remains in place.

aside from the obvious choice of ethan and his nemesis gabriel, grace, benji, luther, paris, kitteridge, ilsa, alanna and even agents degas and briggs all have their own journeys and are transformed by the end of the film.
cruise excels in bringing ethan's journey to a simmering crescendo that questions who he is, who made him and what matters the most.
esai morales' gabriel straddles both morality and humanity, connecting ethan's past and future with a maniacal and devoid-of-humanity turn that would put solomon lane to shame.

regulars simon pegg and ving rhames get an emotional gloss that allows them to punch above their usual range, inviting the audience to lean in and discover what makes them so indispensable to ethan's every escapade.

she matches cruise's charisma and the on-screen chemistry between the thief of artefacts and the retriever is a cat-and-mouse chase you never tire of watching.

with themes reflecting isolation, trust, security, family, artificial intelligence and a world that's rapidly evolving in governance, perceived morality and balance of power, mission: impossible dead reckoning is in itself a huge setup for its impending sequel that cannot arrive soon enough.

mcquarrie delivers in every department be it narrative, action, emotional resonance or visual storytelling, gifting the audience everything it would expect from a summer blockbuster that deserves repeat viewings in as large groups as possible.

how chris mcquarrie, tom cruise and his team will outdo this instalment is beyond me but with action, thrills, and character-defining moments that leap off the screen and embed them into the audience's hearts alongside setpieces that merge the humorous and high-tension, dead reckoning part one is a dead cert for an entertaining reminder of how movies used to be made before the era of cgi-overload.

mission: impossible - dead reckoning part one is the seventh installment in the long-running spy action franchise, and the first part of a two-film finale that promises to wrap up the saga of ethan hunt (tom cruise) and his imf team.

directed by christopher mcquarrie, who also helmed the previous two entries, the film pits hunt against a rogue artificial intelligence called the entity, which threatens to unleash global chaos unless hunt can stop it with the help of a mysterious key.

the film delivers on its promise of spectacular action sequences, stunning locations, and death-defying stunts, all performed by cruise himself with his trademark intensity and charisma.
they are all highlights that showcase mcquarrie's skillful direction and cruise's fearless commitment.

the film also benefits from a strong supporting cast, especially hayley atwell as grace, a skilled thief who becomes hunt's reluctant ally; vanessa kirby as white widow, a black-market arms dealer and broker who has a history with hunt; and the rest of the cast, including rebecca ferguson as ilsa faust, simon pegg as benji dunn, and ving rhames as luther stickell, who deliver excellent performances.

hunt's mission is clear: secure the weapon before it falls into the wrong hands, a task complicated by a web of deceit, shifting alliances, and formidable adversaries.

as the team traverses various exotic locales, from the bustling streets of venice to the icy tundras of norway, the film maintains a relentless pace.

hunt is portrayed not merely as an action hero but as a man burdened by the weight of his responsibilities and the moral complexities of his missions.

cruise's dedication to performing his own stunts adds an authentic edge to the character, making each daring escape and high-speed chase all the more believable.

"dead reckoning part one" explores themes of trust, loyalty, and the moral ambiguities inherent in the world of espionage.

the weapon at the center of the plot symbolizes not just physical destruction but also the potential for misuse of power, echoing contemporary fears about technological advancements and their implications.

the film delves into the personal costs of hunt's mission, questioning the toll such a relentless pursuit of justice takes on one's humanity and relationships.

the plot can be summed up in a few words -- ethan hunt must find a special key to save humanity from an ai entity -- and yet the writers make matters so unnecessarily convoluted that the film winds up at an incredible 2 hours and 43 minutes long, a large percentage of which is far from white-knuckle action.

this leads to some serious pacing issues.

one of the film's key set-pieces -- a car chase in which ethan and the newest imf member grace (hayley atwell) careen about in a yellow fiat 500 -- is played for laughs, which is at odds with the general tone of the franchise.

this entire scene could have been cut from the film without detriment.

cruise's much-touted motorcycle jump off a cliff sees ethan riding his bike at high speed over rough, rocky terrain towards the precipice.

(in reality, cruise pelted along a specially constructed, very smooth ramp, the rocky ground added digitally in post).

in one of the most ridiculous scenes, hunt rescues grace by parachuting through the side of a moving train (this carriage built from balsa wood?), right into a gun toting henchman -- what are the chances?.

a bored programmer with an interest in typography?

preventing the film from being a total disaster are a great turn by pom klementieff as blonde henchwoman paris, the actress stealing every scene she is in despite having next to no dialogue, and an incredible finale in which ethan and grace must race through several of the train's carriages that are dangling over the edge of a bridge, director christopher mcquarrie reminding us a little too late that he can put together an effective action scene.

eric's grade: c 'dead reckoning' is the seventh installment in the tom cruise led 'mission: impossible' franchise.
once again this sees cruise teaming with director and co-writer chistopher mcquarrie who has been solely in the tom cruise business since 2014.

since 2012 nine of the twelve movies mcquarrie has worked on have been tom cruise films, and mcquarrie has really found a career defining niche with the most recent set of 'mission: impossible' films directing 'rogue nation', 'fallout' and now both installments of 'dead reckoning'.

in addition to cruise this latest entry features many returning actors from the franchise including ving rhames, rebecca ferguson, vanessa kirby and simon pegg with new additions such as esai morales, pom klementieff and hayley atwell.

while 'dead reckoning' has cleared over $500 million at the box office that figure becomes a tad less impressive when compared to its $291 million dollar budget which ranks it as one of the most expensive films ever made.

the plot here is chaotic and features a new high tech terrorist that ethan hunt, played by cruise, and his imf team must hunt.

once again ethan and friends must go "rogue", which they even sort of wink at in this film as it does happen in pretty much every 'mission: impossible' film, in order to put an end to this next generation enemy as it becomes apparent that all the governments of the world want to possess the entity to control and use it whereas ethan's small force determines it should be destroyed and are striving to that end.
to start the adventure they must hunt down a key split into two parts.

off to the arabian desert they go to track down key half one which is inexplicably being held by ilsa faust who is now the primary love interest of hunt as well as a disgraced former british spy played by rebecca ferguson.
she spends a great deal of time running away from ethan hunt before, predictably joining up with his cause.
she consistently attempts to run away from ethan falling into malevolent hands each and every time she attempts to flee.

i greatly enjoy the action 'dead reckoning' offers even if it is not breaking new ground, but this is the most convoluted plot and confusing character development that the series has ever had, and we haven't even brushed on the fact that the bad guy the entity has at its beck and call is a nefarious figure from hunt's past.

turn off your brain and enjoy some action as tom cruise runs and runs searching for the latest widget to save the world, but engage your brain at your own risk as 'dead reckoning part one' is a fun, but problematic hot mess.

i grew up watching as a boy the original tv series but have long ago accepted that this cinematic "cruise-controlled" version bears almost no relation to what was originally a tightly-scripted, plot-led and character-driven show.

yes, there are still nods to the source with the use of the theme music, dizzying pre-highlights reel and the masks, my god the masks, but these are perfunctory and what we have now is a pumped-up beyond all recognition stunt-fest staged in exotic locations - this time around say hello to rome, venice and the orient express.

here, ethan and his team are racing around daft trying to track down a new invention called "the entity" which naturally guarantees world domination to its eventual owner.

cue much mayhem as one unlikely action set-piece is piled onto another, including the obligatory crazy motorbike / car-chase, this time around rome, a frantic on-foot pursuit through the side-streets of venice and culminating in mayhem on the orient express, with cruise literally crash-landing to the rescue before the celebrated train goes literally off the rails and down in instalments at the supposed cliff-hanging ending.

for me, it was all way too much and just came across as a massive ego-trip for cruise determined to prove he can still run like the wind (and yes, he gets to run a lot as ever) and personally carry out every other out-there stunt imaginable.

the next impossible mission it seems to me, should he decide to accept it, will be when tom, like the mcu and dcu, has to face up to the realisation that times have changed and that audiences are now fatigued by over-the-top action features like this.

more really is less in this case.

for a very basic overview, final reckoning continues ethan hunt's (tom cruise) search for the "kill switch" to the ai that is running rampant in cyberspace and now gaining access to nuclear arsenals.

so, with grace (hayley atwell) in tow and pals benji (simon pegg) & luther (ving rhames) still supporting him, ethan goes to the depths and the skies to save humanity.

before i get into some of the nit-picking, let me say this: the final reckoning remains a visual and pulse-pounding spectacle.

final reckoning certainly tries to get to those heights (the tom cruise stunts are even wilder than ever before!), but it runs into too many issues and has too much to accomplish (even in a near 3-hour runtime) to be as tight as that peak 2015/2018 era.

we almost enter the territory of magic here with some of the technology, and hunt himself is almost portrayed as a messianic figure.

speaking of which, in this film there are some major world altering events happening, but we don't ever really see the reaction on the streets except briefly in the opening.
the film picks up immediately after the last mission, with ethan hunt holding the key-literally and figuratively-to defeating the entity.

as someone who considers dead reckoning a near-perfect standalone entry in the franchise, i went into this follow-up with excitement dialed up to max-especially with rumors swirling that this might be tom cruise's final outing as hunt.

unfortunately, final reckoning doesn't quite hit the same highs.
tom cruise, as always, is a machine.
if this truly marks cruise's final bow as ethan hunt, it doesn't feel as conclusive or emotionally resonant as it should have.

instead of having an air-right blueprint from which to begin, christopher mcquarrie takes a list of increasingly death-defying stunts curated by tom cruise and figures out a way to staple them together.

the best bits are the little moments in which ethan feels human, showcasing pain or fear or exhaustion, and the brief exchanges that crackle with energy and wit (simon pegg may be neutered, as is everyone else, but he's still the most lively person on screen).
the scenes of ethan running while benji shouts frantic directions in his ear?

sure, there's a brief bout in a submarine, a swift battle in a log cabin, a cut-short pursuit in a tunnel, and a brutal off-screen murder with a meat cleaver, but these snippets of action serve as mere distractions from the relentless exposition and sleepy close-ups and incessant positioning of ethan as a messianic 'chosen one' figure.
ethan hunt clings to the bottom of a plane as it soars through the air, doing loop-de-loops and barrel rolls and straight-up inverted flying in an effort to send him hurtling to an early grave.

although its final beat is somewhat misjudged and it isn't as compelling as it could have been because gabriel is such a whiff of a baddie, it's still an edge-of-your-seat experience that has to be seen to be believed, an impressive feat of filmmaking and stunt work that cements cruise as an adrenaline-fuelled genius and mcquarrie as an all-timer enabler who knows how to capture his star's audacity in the best way possible.
if you're at all interested in seeing cruise risk his life in one of his most terrific temptations of fate to date, then you should go see this on the big screen.

with some momentum lost by a two summer intermission, the second part of tom's final run as ethan hunt is granted some depth by montages from past episodes that remind one not only how much ethan but tom himself has invested his life and soul in the franchise.

but aside from a hilarious callback to the agent who was restationed to alaska in the first mi (and even that joke wears out its welcome thanks to the thudding script), the film staggers under the weight of its profundity, characters unwinding long blank-faced speeches of exposition and ethan's importance as if ai were already running the show.

haley learning to ride sled dogs and the nod to top gun with his landing a plane on the aircraft carrier was cute (surprised they didn't include scenes of him shooting pool, racing a nascar and protesting a war for good measure), but other than one last 'look what tom can still do at sixty-three' rounding of the bases, this is an overlong, over plotted, dire entry for an already dire year in a franchise that probably should have wrapped up two sequels ago.

the third film is probably my favorite of them all because of its gripping emotional storyline, the excellent acting by phillip seymour hoffman who played a chilling and formidable adversary for ethan, and the fact that it single-handedly saved this franchise for me after the disaster of part ii.

i love a good action film as much as any fan, but when there are repeated instances of there being no actual believable way someone could survive the things that ethan did in this movie, it ends up being a detraction from my overall enjoyment more than anything else.
it's clear tom cruise adores his job and loves to make films that cater to audience enjoyment.

mission: impossible--a nearly thirty year old franchise--has only continued to get better.

after a hiccup with 'm:i 2', tom cruise seemed to make it his mission to consistently up the stakes with each new entry, and the results should have created a blueprint for the rest of hollywood.

but as long as we have tom cruise, there'll be at least one true movie star who knows that his job is to entertain his customers.

'mission: impossible - the final reckoning' isn't a perfect movie, and it's not even the best film in the series (that would be 'fallout' in my opinion).

less is more, but the last two entries have set themselves up as the saga's swansong, so it's understandable why they were fooled into thinking they needed things to feel more "epic".

with a reported budget somewhere in the vicinity of $300-$400 million, no one could accuse the final (with what i suspect should come with a very big ?) mission: impossible film from resting on its laurels with collaborative partners tom cruise and his directing buddy christopher mcquarrie giving audiences more of what they've come to expect from one of hollywood's most impressively consistent brands that started out with a bang all the way back in 1996.

working together on the series since 2015's rogue nation and delivering what is considered the best film in the franchise with 2018's fallout entry, mcquarrie and cruise have set themselves a significantly high bar for entertainment and expectations that wasn't quite met commercially with 2023's covid-19 affected dead reckoning and isn't reached with this close to 3 hour epic that provides much in the way of high class spectacle and popcorn munching fun but also feels overly long in the tooth and devoid of early spark, that makes this closing statement on the ethan hunt world an enjoyable one without being an overly memorable one.

following on directly from the events of dead reckoning, final reckoning takes its time to get going as we pay respects to past occurrences dating all the way back to hunt's first foray into the world of the imf while also setting in motion the key elements of this journeys plot, that basically sees the world teetering on the edge of implosion with a dangerous a.

i system wrecking havoc across the globe with only hunt and his ever willing team of compatriots able to potentially save the day.

hoping to prove to us for an eighth time that these missions are in fact possible, cruise's hunt must traverse the lonely late night streets of london, negotiate with presidents, go for some ice cold dips in the ocean and enjoy a precarious joy ride in the skies if he is to overcome the odds and conquer evil for those he will never know yet while cruise is ever willing at the age of 62, there's something slightly underwhelming about much of final reckoning's first 90 or so minutes that only really begin to reach the levels we have become accustomed too around the half-way mark, making this the type of big screen experience you're likely to ever only seek out for one go around.

it's absolutely the equivalent of first world problems in a viewing manner when you can sit back and not be overcome with joy and wow-factor by a team so committed to providing large-scale spectacle and amusement but when you take the time and consider what the first part of final reckoning entails, you can't help but escape the feeling cruise and mcquarrie overestimated the work they were doing, with final reckoning likely to have benefited greatly from stronger early set-pieces, less heavy-handed dialogue and a tighter edit to enhance the overall feeling of the film weighed up as a whole.

there's still no denying that when the film hits its marks it hits as well as any other big budget blockbuster could muster, a thrilling final stretch will make you sit back with a giant smile on your face while cruise's unmatched commitment to his role as an entertainer and some emotionally charged character movements will work well for the series long-term fans but there's an underlying sense that final reckoning is slightly on the wrong side of self-indulgence and mis-guided confidence, something that wasn't such a factor in the series peaks of entries 3 - 7.

if final reckoning does indeed end up being the final bow for cruise and his impossible gang we can be thankful for the quality years of viewing experiences we've been given courtesy of their pride in providing cinema fans a reason to celebrate the big screen blockbuster experience and while this "farewell" doesn't end with a mighty bang, there's still enough reason for fans to support one last go around the sun for one of film histories most surprisingly consistent and likable properties.

final say -

unable to overcome its more indulgent nature in all instances, if you can suspend your disbelief sufficiently mission: impossible - the final reckoning is still top quality hollywood filmmaking that might not match the best of its namesakes but still gives us plenty to enjoy along its way to a breath-taking final stretch.

"mission: impossible - the final reckoning": a thrilling, yet exhausting, finale "mission: impossible - the final reckoning" arrives with the weight of expectation, not just as the latest installment in a beloved franchise, but as the purported grand finale to ethan hunt's incredible journey.

and while it undeniably delivers on the series' hallmark of breathtaking stunts and relentless action, it also shows signs of a franchise reaching its limits, for better or worse.

picking up directly from "dead reckoning part one," the film thrusts ethan hunt (tom cruise, as committed as ever) and his imf team into a race against time to neutralize "the entity," a rogue, sentient ai threatening to plunge the world into nuclear chaos.

this formidable new antagonist, combined with the return of gabriel (esai morales), a mysterious figure from ethan's past, attempts to bring together decades of narrative threads, aiming for a truly comprehensive conclusion.

the action sequences are, as always, the undeniable highlight.
tom cruise's dedication to performing his own death-defying feats remains unparalleled, and it's a genuine marvel to witness.

the villain, gabriel, despite his critical role, could have benefited from a deeper exploration of his connection to ethan.

ultimately, "mission: impossible - the final reckoning" is a rollercoaster ride of epic proportions.

it's a testament to tom cruise's unwavering dedication and christopher mcquarrie's visionary direction that even with its occasional narrative stumbles, the film remains an incredibly entertaining and visually stunning experience.

while it aims for a definitive ending, the film leaves just enough room for speculation, proving that the mission, for ethan hunt, might truly be impossible to conclude.

verdict: a high-octane, visually spectacular, if occasionally overstuffed, finale that delivers the adrenaline-pumping action fans have come to expect from the "mission: impossible" franchise.
a worthy send-off for ethan hunt, even if the "final reckoning" feels a little less "final" than advertised.

tom cruise delivers a high-octane farewell in mission: impossible - the final reckoning, the eighth and final installment of the long-running franchise.

directed by christopher mcquarrie, the film sees imf agent ethan hunt confronting his most formidable adversary yet: a rogue ai known as the entity, capable of global annihilation.

the film is a spectacle of practical stunts and action sequences, including a tense underwater submarine scene and a daring biplane sequence, showcasing cruise's commitment to performing his own stunts.
